children: A number of stocks fell in the afternoon session after artificial intelligence and semiconductor stocks pulled back from the previous session's sharp rally, dragging down technology-heavy indexes. CNBC reported that the Nasdaq Composite fell 2.5% and the S&P 500 declined 1.2%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average traded around the flatline. Nvidia shares dropped more than 7% after surging 31% in the previous session following Jensen Huang's return as CEO, while Anthropic shares fell 9%, breaking below its IPO price.

Tom Hulick, CEO of Strategy Asset Managers, told CNBC that Nvidia still has "a lot of things to worry about" regarding corporate governance. Mark Haefele, chief investment officer at UBS Global Wealth Management, said in a note that he expects greater differentiation between established platforms and companies dependent on debt, scarce capacity or continued speculative growth.

A pullback in artificial intelligence and semiconductor stocks can weigh on industrial companies that supply manufacturing equipment, electronic components or power systems for data centers. Share prices across a sector often decline together when investors reduce exposure to capital spending themes and turn more selective on growth.
The stock market overreacts to news, and big price drops can present good opportunities to buy high-quality stocks.
Among others, the following stocks were impacted:

Innio’s shares are extremely volatile and have had 45 moves greater than 5% over the last year. In that context, today’s move indicates the market considers this news meaningful but not something that would fundamentally change its perception of the business.

The previous big move we wrote about was 8 days ago when the stock dropped 3.4% on the news that the Commerce Department’s crackdown on Chinese firms leasing Nvidia computing power from foreign data centers raised demand concerns for future power and cooling deployments, adding to rising bond yields, post-election permitting worries, and Nvidia’s leadership crisis ahead of its earnings report. Infrastructure suppliers have faced multiple compression since Democratic midterm victories raised permitting risks in hubs like Texas, roughly 25% of U.S. data-center construction, per Bernstein research cited by CNBC, while October’s 6.5% annual producer price jump drove 10-year yields to 5.17% in the previous session.

When Nvidia reports third-quarter results later in the week, commentary on its Vera Rubin rack ramp and prior 70% fiscal 2028 growth outlook will test buildout pacing alongside the new third-country restrictions. Data-center power and cooling suppliers sit between the utility grid and the GPU rack. Because their multiples capitalize multi-year density upgrades, tighter rules on overseas AI clusters or any hesitation in Nvidia’s next-generation rack timeline weighs on the group regardless of current demand.

Innio is down 64% since the beginning of the year, and at $11.98 per share, it is trading 70.9% below its 52-week high of $41.13 from June 2026. Investors who bought $1,000 worth of Innio’s shares at the IPO in June 2026 would now be looking at an investment worth $359.64.

Nvidia’s chips cost a hundred grand. The connectors that make them work cost even more. One company makes them all.

Every AI server needs specialized infrastructure the chip companies don’t make. High-speed cables. Power connectors. Thermal sensors. This 90-year-old company built a monopoly on it. The AI boom just started. This stock is still flying under the radar.
